extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing effective newspaper leads: what information to include, what to omit, the tone and accuracy required, and the grammatical forms (12 lead forms plus informal and special leads) appropriate for various story types.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Lead Should Not Be Overburdened
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should never be burdened with minor details; if the whole story is told in the lead, nothing more should be written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compression is of primary importance; avoid repetition. A lead overloaded with particulars 'steals all its thunder' from the body. Prefer several short emphatic sentences to one long involved opening that attempts to tell everything at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liveliness Improves the Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A touch of human interest or liveliness brightens dull stories and may attract readers who are weary of stereotyped openings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal or slightly vivid phrasing when appropriate (example: playful rewrite of a Women’s league reception lead). Avoid being far-fetched or strained; liveliness should color facts without sacrificing accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Lead Must Be Complete
rubrics_metrics.description: The summarizing lead should answer all fundamental questions about the event it records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be a who, a what, a when, and a where in every story; include why and how when relevant. Include just enough information to establish each point clearly (e.g., class, school name, city) but omit unnecessary particulars such as parents' names, exact seat numbers, etc. Remember lead establishes gist; body supplies details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose Which Point to Feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which element of the story (who, why, what, how, when, where) is most striking and place it to feature in the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and place are usually secondary; do not put unimportant points before the startling information. If in doubt about which point to feature, consult the city editor; otherwise study the facts intelligently to select the emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Monotonous Openings; Opening Word Should Be Significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reporters overwork names or articles as first words; the opening word should be significant or interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually bad form to begin with an article (a, an, the) or with temporal adverbs like yesterday/today/recently. Use variety in grammatical forms to avoid trite openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Simple Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a story with a single impressive fact stated emphatically in a few words, the simple-statement lead is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually begins with a name or important common noun; terse, direct sentences are most effective (examples: 'Theodore Roosevelt is dead.' 'President Harding is dead.'). Leave details to the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Series of Simple Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful in action stories to play up several competing features at once by use of short sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the broken, choppy 'bing-bing-bing' style. Maintain smooth movement and even tone by clever ordering of sentence elements. Example: a sequence describing last-minute forward passes, score, and key player actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Substantive Clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal for putting decisions, beliefs, opinions, indirect questions, and indirect quotations at the beginning of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form to bring the feature (decision, belief, question, quote) to the fore rather than burying it under boilerplate meeting-reporting phrasing. Examples include leads beginning with 'That schools should be closed...' or 'Whether Patterson is to have a new swimming tank...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Conditional Clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conditional ('if') clauses when humorous effect is desired or when significant conditions and their probable results are to be featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good for speculative or hypothetical sport stories and for humorous openings; examples show hypothetical consequences driving interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Causal Clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences starting with because or since emphasize causes and motives, which are often the most interesting features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring causes/motives to the fore, but be cautioned against overworking causal leads; use sparingly and appropriately with clear example sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Purpose Clause / Infinitive Phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: When purpose is the most important feature, begin with a purpose clause or (more commonly) an infinitive phrase to play up purpose elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infinitive phrases are more frequent and concise; purpose clauses can sound formal and cumbersome. Examples provided; avoid long 'in order that' constructions in newspaper leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Concessive Clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Used to introduce stories where a person has succeeded despite overwhelming difficulties; brings out that feature effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin leads with 'Although' or 'Though' to emphasize success over hardship (examples of athletes or individuals overcoming injury or disadvantage).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Temporal Clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely used; employ temporal clauses only when the time of occurrence is more important than the occurrence itself or must be given before the occurrence can be understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show 'When the pool is completed...' or 'After X had scored...'; use sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Infinitive Phrase (as distinct form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinitive leads emphasize purpose or verbal ideas in a forceful, economical way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillful infinitive leads can add dramatic force while keeping economy of words (example: 'To fall 4000 feet with a torn and useless parachute and yet to escape injury...').

rubrics_metrics.name: The Participial Phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Best for indicating method, manner, or attendant circumstances which are of primary importance in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use participial phrases to feature the manner of an event (examples: 'Digging his way through a stone wall...' or football plays begun with participial phrasing).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Prepositional Phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A good medium for featuring means or method by which something is done and useful for playing up causes and motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'With a soup spoon for a shovel Tom McPhee...' or 'By a 45-yard drop kick...'; use to foreground method/means.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Absolute Construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A construction (noun + participle or adjective) useful for featuring underlying causes and motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Somewhat difficult to master but valuable; examples: 'His money gone, and his health broken, Tim Flaherty...'. Use to compactly present circumstances that explain the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal Leads (general guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal leads are difficult to write and should be used sparingly by student reporters; combine informal style with a summarizing form if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware 'featuritis'—overworking informal lead types so that the story ceases to be news. The chapter treats four informal types (question, verse, startling quotation, suspense) with examples and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Question Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A question used as an opening; generally bad form for straight news stories but can be effective for strong feature-interest stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violates 'Don't ask 'em; tell 'em' rule for straight news. Use when a question genuinely increases curiosity and is appropriate for feature-style pieces (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Verse Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening with original verse or a quotation of verse; seldom recommended for average reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original verse is beyond average capability and quotations are often trite; use rarely and only when suited to the piece (example provided where light doggerel worked for a feature).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Startling Quotation Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening with a startling verbatim quotation; one of the easiest and most effective informal leads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good orator or speaker's striking statement can instantly catch attention; use such quotations freely when available (examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Suspense Lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead that withholds outcome to create suspense; exceedingly difficult and recommended only for experienced writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid for beginners and use only when the story would be ruined by revealing the outcome early. Example shows narrative suspense for a feature story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Leads / Boxed Summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: For long or complicated stories a boxed summary or striking quotation (a 'box' at the beginning) may be placed before a secondary lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boxed leads are seldom necessary in high-school papers and editors avoid frequent use because they stiffen page appearance. Use only when features cannot be effectively played up in an ordinary lead; follow box with suitable secondary lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy the First Requisite
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead must be perfectly clear and true in every detail; accuracy takes precedence over striking effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misleading statements even if corrected later; better to understate than to exaggerate. The lead should establish appropriate tone (funny, pathetic, dramatic) consistent with the body. Final tests: Is it accurate? Is it interesting? Is it in keeping with the rest of the story?

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Sacrifice Tone or Appropriateness for Cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should establish an atmosphere or tone matching the story; avoid facetious leads for serious events and mock-pathos for funny stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mismatched tone undermines effect; reporters should not write facetious leads for tragic stories or overly sentimental openings for humorous pieces.
